categories.label: Contract-Trust Complementarity and Relational Governance Models
categories.memo: Covers how formal contractual governance and informal trust-based governance interact, complement, and evolve across project stages in MMC/OSC projects.

codes.label: Dual governance (contract + trust)
codes.description: Combining formal contract governance with trust-based relational governance is more effective than either alone for managing inter-organizational coordination in OSC projects.

sub_codes.label: Stage-based evolution of governance
sub_codes.description: Contract governance is more important early in the project to establish structure, while trust becomes more critical as the project progresses to resolve emerging conflicts.

sub_codes.label: Structure-governance fit
sub_codes.description: Vertical/hierarchical organizational structures pair better with contract governance, while flat/integrated structures pair better with trust governance.

codes.label: Contract incompleteness and informal governance
codes.description: Because contracts cannot fully specify all OSC-specific contingencies, informal governance based on trust emerges to manage out-of-contract work arising from design changes.

codes.label: One-off contracting undermining trust
codes.description: Short-term, one-off bidding-based contracting discourages the development of deep trust between parties, increasing opportunistic behavior and reducing collaborative performance.

codes.label: Industry-wide distrust as adoption barrier
codes.description: Lack of trust and reluctance to embrace new prefabrication techniques, compounded by poor education and lack of reliable comparison tools, hampers wider industry adoption.

categories.label: Collaborative and Integrated Delivery Methods as Relational Mechanisms
categories.memo: Addresses how IPD, alliancing, design-build and other integrated delivery structures function as relational governance tools that enable collaboration in MMC/prefabrication contexts.

codes.label: IPD/alliancing core features
codes.description: Multiparty agreements, shared risk/reward, and early involvement of all parties define IPD and similar relational contracts, aligning stakeholder incentives toward project outcomes.

codes.label: Collaborative behaviors under alliance/IPD structures
codes.description: Self-managing teams, open-mindedness toward problem resolution, and a shift from hierarchical to team-based decision-making ('best for project') characterize effective collaboration within integrated delivery arrangements.

codes.label: Procurement strategy shaping collaboration
codes.description: The choice of procurement/delivery method is seen by practitioners as directly influencing the level of collaboration achievable on a project.

codes.label: IPD/DfMA synergy
codes.description: DfMA (product/process integration) needs to be paired with IPD (people integration) contractual frameworks to achieve full integration; standard IPD forms like CCDC30 exist but require further contractual refinement for DfMA/offsite synergy.

codes.label: Design-build proximity effects
codes.description: Design-Build and similar integrated procurement approaches increase proximity between design and construction parties, improving performance metrics relative to Design-Bid-Build, and are sometimes rated the most prefabrication-friendly delivery method.

codes.label: IPD as beneficial but not prerequisite
codes.description: IPD/integrated teams can improve prefabrication outcomes but are not strictly necessary, particularly where performance-based specifications already allow flexibility without full integration.

codes.label: Comparative performance of relational vs. traditional delivery
codes.description: Case evidence shows integrated/hybrid delivery (design-build/IPD) leads to smoother implementation and fewer change orders compared to traditional design-bid-build subcontracting.

codes.label: Innovative risk/reward-sharing contract models
codes.description: Advocacy for new contractual models that share risks, responsibilities, profits and expenses among parties as a way to enable OSC adoption and strengthen partnerships.

categories.label: Early Involvement and Design-Phase Collaboration
categories.memo: Focuses on the timing and structure of stakeholder involvement, particularly contractors, suppliers, and fabricators, during design as a preventive collaborative mechanism.

codes.label: Early contractor/supplier involvement in design
codes.description: Involving contractors, suppliers, or fabricators early in design—sometimes even prior to formal contract—prevents unbuildable or costly designs and reduces later conflicts and delays.

codes.label: Consequences of exclusion from design
codes.description: Excluding contractors or suppliers from the design process leads to conflicts, design changes, and project delays, illustrating the risk of inadequate collaborative structuring.

codes.label: Avoiding disconnects across design/contract phase transitions
codes.description: Sustained collaboration among owner, architect, and contractor must be maintained across contractual transitions between assessment, basic design, and detailed design phases to avoid critical failures.

codes.label: Design freeze and change order limitations
codes.description: Early manufacturing start and design inflexibility in modular/OSC projects limit the ability to accommodate late changes, making design freeze and coordinated timing of involvement critical success factors.

codes.label: IP protection tensions in early collaboration
codes.description: Suppliers may withhold detailed technical information (e.g., shop drawings) to protect intellectual property until a formal subcontract is secured, creating friction with the goal of early collaborative involvement.

categories.label: Communication, Information-Sharing and Digital Collaboration Protocols
categories.memo: Covers contractual and technological mechanisms for enabling timely communication and information exchange as a preventive governance mechanism.

codes.label: Absence of communication-promoting contract terms as risk
codes.description: Lack of contractual terms promoting efficient communication and collaboration is identified as a primary contractual risk in modular/MMC projects, with slow submittal/RFI turnaround being a central dispute driver.

codes.label: Data-sharing and BIM protocols in IPD contracts
codes.description: Formalized contractual provisions requiring parties to agree on software platforms and data-sharing protocols to support timely and relevant information exchange.

codes.label: Digital technology as collaboration enabler
codes.description: BIM, cloud platforms, digital twins, and communication technologies facilitate smoother collaborative workflows and coordination between offsite/onsite and design/construction parties, with human factors (e.g., personality traits within BIM processes) also shaping outcomes.

codes.label: Communication breakdown from subcontracting separation
codes.description: Financial and organizational separation created by traditional design-build/lump-sum subcontracting with offsite factories leads to minimal communication during manufacturing and late disruptive design changes.

categories.label: Supply Chain and Multi-Actor Coordination
categories.memo: Addresses coordination challenges and collaborative mechanisms across supply chain actors, including suppliers, manufacturers, vendors, logistics providers, and subcontractors.

codes.label: Reduced actor count via integrated supplier-builder systems
codes.description: Prefabricated/integrated supplier-builder systems and vertical integration reduce the number of contractual relationships needed, simplifying coordination compared to fragmented traditional subcontracting.

codes.label: Vendor/manufacturer partnership agreements
codes.description: Formal or quasi-formal (sometimes nonbinding) partnership agreements with vendors and manufacturers cover communication, logistics, materials, payment, and training, functioning as relational governance supplementing formal contracts.

codes.label: Coordination across dual/split design responsibility
codes.description: Coordination between separate structural engineers (design engineer and supplier/fabricator engineer) is required to ensure specified elements are producible, reflecting a division of design responsibility tied to prefabrication.

codes.label: Logistics service modularization and multi-actor coordination
codes.description: Modularizing logistics services simplifies service content but increases the number of actors requiring coordination, creating a need for an authoritative actor (e.g., main contractor) to coordinate across service module providers.

codes.label: Mandatory/non-voluntary supply chain participation
codes.description: Contractually mandated use of logistics service modules by subcontractors (as non-voluntary customers) excludes them from co-creation and reduces trust, commitment, and perceived value.

codes.label: Risk transfer upstream in supply chains
codes.description: Construction supply chains show a tendency to transfer value/supply chain risks upstream to subcontractors and suppliers, damaging trust, reliability, and collaborative commitment.

codes.label: Repeated/temporary procurement limiting continuity
codes.description: The temporary nature of construction projects means logistics/supply chain relationships and trust-building must restart with each new project, limiting the benefits of accumulated collaborative experience.

codes.label: Synchronizing offsite fabrication with onsite construction
codes.description: Coordinating offsite factory production schedules with onsite construction sequencing is essential to avoid cascading delays and cost overruns, requiring collaborative scheduling provisions between parties.

categories.label: Labor Relations and Union Collaboration
categories.memo: Addresses the role of labor unions as a distinct relational governance dimension affecting prefabrication adoption.

codes.label: Union resistance to prefabrication/outsourcing
codes.description: Labor union relations and resistance (e.g., fear of reduced work hours) can constrain or discourage contractors from adopting prefabrication and outsourcing fabrication work.

codes.label: Mitigating union resistance through experience and catalog strategies
codes.description: Contractors with existing prefabrication facilities experience less union resistance, and manufacturers use catalog/product framing strategies to help comply with union constraints, suggesting relational approaches to managing labor tensions.

codes.label: Need for contractual/labor policy innovation
codes.description: Future contractual strategies, such as prefabrication outsourcing agreements and labor portability between union locals, are recommended to resolve union-contractor tensions collaboratively.

categories.label: Collaboration Failure Modes and Dispute Linkages
categories.memo: Covers how breakdowns in collaboration and relational governance manifest as contractual disputes, distinguishing preventive collaboration failures from Theme 2's broader dispute focus.

codes.label: Co-occurrence of interconnected collaboration failures
codes.description: Disputes in modular/MMC projects typically arise from the co-occurrence of multiple interconnected causes (e.g., poor communication, coordination failures, delays) rather than isolated factors, implying contracts must address clusters of relational risk together.

codes.label: Contractual risk/disputes as performance-critical factors
codes.description: Contractual risks and disputes rank among the most critical factors affecting both cost and schedule performance in modular projects, underscoring the performance stakes of poor relational governance.

codes.label: Stakeholder misalignment on risk perception
codes.description: Significant misalignment among owners, consultants, contractors, and subcontractors regarding which risks are most critical suggests a need for collaborative processes to build shared understanding and risk allocation.

codes.label: Onerous subcontract terms undermining collaboration
codes.description: Powerful Tier One builders sometimes impose rigid subcontract terms leaving suppliers with little negotiating power, straining collaborative relationships despite contractual compliance.
